title: The Education Gadfly Weekly: Missouri Charter Funding, Ohio Credentials, and the CLT Graduation Loophole
author: Thomas B. Fordham Institute
source: The Education Gadfly Weekly, Volume 26, Number 32 (fordhaminstitute.org), August 13, 2026
summary: The August 13, 2026 Education Gadfly Weekly, published by the Thomas B. Fordham Institute, bundles several short-form policy analyses with the digest's own editorial framing. The lead item, by Amber Northern and Michael Petrilli, reports that Missouri's 2022 charter-funding law delivered a real infusion of dollars to Kansas City and St. Louis charter schools but that the state's underlying funding formula still fails to send local dollars to the public schools students actually attend, so the equity problem persists in a narrowed form. A second item by Aaron Churchill covers Ohio's decision to cut its state-approved industry-credential list from more than 700 entries to 126, using workforce data to stop credentials from being used as graduation shortcuts with little labor-market value. A third item by Charles Barone raises validity concerns about Florida's rapid embrace of the Classic Learning Test, reporting that the exam is increasingly functioning as a low-bar workaround for students who can't clear the state's regular graduation assessments. A closing item on a Kentucky co-requisite remediation program shows modest gains when underprepared community-college students are supported inside credit-bearing courses rather than routed through standalone remedial classes first. Taken together, the issue's throughline is that well-intentioned reforms - funding formulas, credential lists, and alternative assessments - keep drifting away from their original accountability purpose without deliberate maintenance.
points: Missouri's 2022 charter-funding law narrowed but did not close the local-dollar funding gap between charter and district schools, because the underlying formula still doesn't send local dollars to the schools students actually attend.

Ohio slashed its state-approved industry-credential list from more than 700 to 126, using workforce data to stop credentials from functioning as graduation shortcuts disconnected from real labor-market value.
Reporting cited in the digest found Florida's Classic Learning Test is increasingly used as a low-bar graduation workaround for students who can't clear the state's own reading and math requirements.

A Kentucky co-requisite remediation model — placing underprepared students directly into credit-bearing courses with support rather than standalone remedial classes — shows modest measurable benefits.
quotes: Missouri's 2022 charter funding law delivered a major infusion of dollars to public charter schools in Kansas City and St. Louis, helping offset much of a longstanding gap. But a new Fordham analysis shows that the underlying formula continues to recreate the inequity it was meant to solve.
True funding fairness will require local dollars to follow students to the public schools they actually attend.

Like many states, Ohio has encouraged students to attain industry-recognized credentials, but too many became graduation shortcuts rather than solid labor-market signals. A new state overhaul cuts the approved list from more than 700 credentials to 126 and uses workforce data to focus schools on those with real value.
The Classic Learning Test is spreading rapidly, but new reporting raises serious questions about whether it is rigorous enough to serve as a graduation, admissions, or scholarship gatekeeper.
In Florida, for example, the exam appears to be functioning less as a college-readiness measure than as a workaround for students who cannot clear the state's reading and math bars.

Students who arrive at community college unprepared for college-level work often face extra remedial courses that cost time and money without moving them closer to degrees. A new approach in Kentucky gives some students support while they take credit-bearing classes, and recent research suggests that modest benefits follow.
